I have been farming my land in Quzhou County for over forty years. I am sixty-seven now, and though I never went to school, I know this land and its seasons by heart. My family has about eight mu of good flat land on the North China Plain, and around here, everyone follows the wheat-maize rotation. That is what feeds us and what the market buys, so I will not gamble with strange crops.

This autumn, I will sow winter wheat on all eight mu. I will use an improved variety—probably *Luyuan 502* or *Jimai 22*—because these are the seeds my neighbors trust and the grain station sells. Before sowing in early October, I will run the rotary tiller to prepare the seedbed. For fertilizer, I will spread about one hundred jin of compound fertilizer as a basal dose, and when spring comes I will topdress with urea at green-up and jointing stages. In total, that works out to roughly sixty-five jin of nitrogen, twenty-two jin of phosphate, and eight jin of potash per mu. I will irrigate three or four times: winter irrigation once to protect against the cold, and then two or three times in spring depending on the rainfall. I usually spray pesticides four times for wheat—to control aphids, rust, and weeds. If the weather cooperates, I expect about one thousand jin of wheat per mu.

As soon as the wheat comes off the combine in early June, I will plant summer maize the same day or the next. Time is short, so I will plant directly into the wheat stubble without ploughing—no-tillage saves fuel and labor, and the crop still grows fine. I will sow a hybrid variety, *Denghai 605*, which gives good yield and is easy to buy. For maize I use less fertilizer than wheat: about eighty jin of compound fertilizer at sowing, giving roughly twenty-two jin of nitrogen, six jin of phosphate, and six jin of potash per mu. Maize needs less irrigation because the summer rains usually help, so I will water twice—once at sowing to ensure emergence, and once at the big-flush stage if it turns dry. I will spray pesticides three or four times, mainly for corn borer and weeds. I expect about eleven hundred jin of maize per mu if the summer storms do not flatten it.

That is my plan. Wheat in winter, maize in summer, on the same eight mu. It is the safe choice, and at my age, safe is what I need.
